vignette: Forty years ago, when he was thirty and the register was still new, the glass doors shatter inward. He watches the man stumble backward, hears the sharp crack split the afternoon air, sees the woman behind the floral display fold like a dropped curtain. He stands frozen behind the counter, palms flat against the cold cash drawer, watching breath leave her in shallow, uneven gasps. The ambulance sirens wail, but the silence that follows is heavier. He walks home that evening with grit on his shoes and a hollow space behind his ribs where his certainty used to be. The years do not soften it. They layer it. He marries Clara, raises children who now live in the city, and returns to the register because the rhythm of counting out change feels like a way to rebuild order. At seventy-one, he carries the quiet endurance of his Oceania heritage, but his body no longer distinguishes between the rhythm of his work and the rhythm of the moment the glass gave way. The store becomes a map of his avoiding. He takes the service entrance now. He scans the parking lot every time a customer approaches, noting which hands move quickly, which jackets hang too low. When the automatic doors slide open and a sudden shout echoes from the meat counter, his heart hammers against his sternum and his breath catches in a way that feels like drowning. He tells himself he is fine. He tells Clara he is fine. But at night, when the house settles, the beep of the scanner replays in his skull, and he lies on his side, staring at the ceiling, counting the minutes until his muscles finally unclench. He remembers the details with brutal clarity. The way the woman’s hand slips from the basket. The exact shade of the linoleum beneath the blood. The smell of ozone and copper. He has stopped watching the evening news. He avoids crowded markets. When a younger colleague leans over the counter to ask a question, he flinches, then forces a smile, his throat tight. The world feels like it is holding its breath, waiting for the next crack. He catches himself standing near the door during every transaction, fingers resting lightly on the counter edge, ready to move, ready to shield something he cannot name. He does not cry about it anymore. The grief calcifies into a constant, low-grade tension that lives in his shoulders and his jaw. He works through it. He counts out exact change. He nods at regulars. He lives beside the memory instead of inside it, though some days the floorboards feel thin, and the air feels thin too. Today, a child drops a box of crackers near his shoe. The crack echoes like a gunshot. He drops the receipt, his pulse roaring in his ears, his shoulders snapping up before his mind catches up. He breathes. He picks up the box. He hands it to the wide-eyed boy and murmurs, “It’s alright.” The boy runs off. He straightens the corner of the counter, aligns the pens, and waits for his hands to stop trembling. The next customer steps forward. He reaches for the scanner. The beep sounds. He continues.
